copyright: People rowing among colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China (© Jackal Pan/Getty Images)
description: People paddle through a glowing maze of bald cypress in Xuancheng, Anhui, where autumn transforms flooded woodlands into a tapestry of amber, copper and deep rust. Known scientifically as 'Taxodium distichum', bald cypress is unusual among conifers because it sheds its soft, feathery needles each fall, turning reddish-brown before they drop.

copyright: Taquaras Beach, Balneário Camboriú, Brazil (© MaRabelo/Getty Images)
description: On Brazil's southern coast, Taquaras Beach offers a quieter escape in Balneário Camboriú, Santa Catarina. Clear blue-green waters meet a broad stretch of golden sand, backed by lush vegetation and rolling green hills. Away from the livelier atmosphere of the city centre, the beach is known for its peaceful surroundings and natural beauty. With its inviting shoreline, rich greenery and unspoilt feel, Taquaras showcases a calmer side of this popular Brazilian coastal destination.

copyright: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada (© Danita Delimont/Adobe Stock)
description: These polar bears are gathering along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, Canada, waiting for sea ice to form so they can head back out to hunt seals. Polar bears are powerful swimmers, expert hunters and remarkably adapted to life in one of Earth's harshest environments. Yet shrinking sea ice means many spend longer on land, making it harder to find food and raising the risk of encounters with people.

copyright: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany (© Britus/Getty Images)
description: Today we're enjoying the misty views sweeping across the Black Forest, which stretches for around 160 kilometres across south-west Germany, bringing together wooded hills, deep valleys, lakes and charming towns. Its highest point, Feldberg, rises to 1,493 metres, while the Black Forest is also the starting point for the Danube and Neckar rivers. There's plenty of history and tradition here too. Forestry has long played an important role in the region, while its centuries-old clockmaking heritage helped make the distinctive cuckoo clock famous far beyond Germany.

copyright: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy (© leonid_tit/Getty Images)
description: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

copyright: Sandhill cranes, Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, New Mexico, USA (© Terry St.Louis/Getty Images)
description: Winter brings a familiar rhythm to Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge in New Mexico. The cranes arrive, wetlands fill with birds and this area becomes a hub for seasonal wildlife. Established in 1939, the 57,331-acre sanctuary was created to provide a protected stopover for migrating waterfowl. Its wetlands, fields and waterways now support wildlife throughout the year. Sandhill cranes, seen in today's image, are especially associated with the refuge during winter.

copyright: Standing stones at Avebury in Wiltshire, England (© George W Johnson/Getty Images)
description: As morning mist drifts among the standing stones of Avebury in Wiltshire, England, the scene feels almost timeless. These ancient megaliths form part of one of the world's most remarkable prehistoric landscapes, centred on a vast Neolithic monument built around 4,500 years ago. Avebury contains the world's largest prehistoric stone circle, as well as a massive henge and stone avenues extending into the surrounding countryside. Together with nearby monuments such as Silbury Hill and West Kennet Avenue, it forms part of an extensive Neolithic complex that has fascinated generations of visitors, researchers and archaeologists.
